title: Constitution Week, 2025
summary:
The White House has proclaimed September 17–23, 2025 as Constitution Week, marking 238 years since the Constitution was signed and calling for a renewed focus on civic education, patriotism, and safeguarding the nation’s founding principles.

The proclamation urges teachers and local leaders to teach students about the rights and duties of citizenship. It also highlights recent actions the administration says are meant to elevate traditional civic values: promoting a particular view of American history in museums and schools, expanding parental control in education, ending diversity, equity, and inclusion programs in federal agencies, and directing prosecutions for desecrating the American flag. The message ties these steps to honoring the Constitution and preparing for the 250th anniversary of American independence next year.

People who prioritize civics instruction, national symbols, and a more uniform approach to teaching American history may welcome this. Parents who want more influence over curricula, and those who oppose diversity and inclusion initiatives in government, may also see it as a win. Educators looking for a clear moment to spotlight constitutional rights and responsibilities could find the week a useful rallying point.

Others may have concerns. Supporters of diversity and inclusion efforts may view the move to end such programs as a setback for workplace equity. Free speech advocates could worry that steps to prosecute flag desecration conflict with protected expression. Some teachers and historians may see risks in prescribing how history should be taught, fearing politics could crowd out academic judgment or the full complexity of America’s story. And the proclamation’s sharp language toward critics may strike some as polarizing in a moment that calls for civic unity.

At its core, Constitution Week is an invitation to engage with the country’s founding document. How it’s carried out—and who feels included—will shape its impact.
